rv.q: The show is a competently crafted jukebox musical that tells the story of Florence Greenberg
But she didn’t tell me there would be quite so many, or that any one of them could be this dismal.
"Baby It's You!" is not one of those exceptions.
The story they tell might well be true-to-life, but it comes across as stilted and unlikely.
The show takes some of the great American pop tunes of the 20th century and homogenizes their transcendent joys and heartaches into bland karaoke.
There’s a remarkable story here, but you’d be forgiven for missing it: The writers certainly have.
If you are looking for a night out that is easy on the ear and the brain, then, baby, Baby It's You is for you.
The show works best when it focuses on the music itself rather than trying to shoehorn in a storyline
Leavel elevates the enterprise with pitch-perfect singing, acting and bouffant, her Florence blowzy and vulnerable.
Unfortunately, Baby It's You's attempt to sandwich Greenberg's story into what is essentially a glitzy concert fall flat.

If your show is in trouble, be sure to get Beth Leavel in your cast...With subtle humor, expert timing, and knockout pipes, Leavel strives mightily to bring this mishmash of a rock tuner up to her level, but she can't perform miracles. There is an audience for this kind of show...
Clearly, the writers' interest in the group only extends so far.

But the Shirelles, one of the greatest girl groups of all time (heck, they were covered by the Beatles), get a show of such total ineptitude and cynical profiteering that your mouth pretty much dangles open in disbelief for the duration of the entire tawdry proceedings.
Quite an extraordinary woman, quite a fascinating and entertaining play.

cn.t: Critics find this jukebox musical about the Shirelles and manager Florence Greenberg unfocused and artless, with a weak narrative that can't decide whose story it's telling. Beth Leavel's performance earns praise in an otherwise disappointing show.

sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name Center Orchestra rows D-K as the house sweet spot; Broadhurst's mezzanine overhang does not begin cutting the stage picture until row K, so D-K sits entirely in front of the overhang line while still clearing the shallow front-row rake. SeatPlan editors specifically advise skipping rows A-C because the Broadhurst stage pushes action to the sides that front-row patrons miss.

Broadhurst's mezzanine overhang begins at row K and, per Headout and SeatPlan, 'visibly cuts into the top of the stage by row R' - specifically blocking projections and anything that plays high. The rake in these rear orchestra rows is also called out as shallow, compounding the loss of vertical stage picture.

SeatPlan specifically flags the Broadhurst's Left and Right Boxes as overhanging far-aisle orchestra seats around rows D-F, cutting off the corresponding side of the stage, and the three elevated boxes themselves 'sit at quite sharp angles' with unfixed chairs. Headout adds that double-digit seats near the aisle get only partial views of the stage.

Multiple sources (Headout, SeatPlan, NewYorkTheatreGuide) call Center Mezzanine rows A-B the second-best location in the house. The Broadhurst's front mezzanine ledge has no railing, so shorter patrons aren't blocked - a Broadhurst-specific quirk noted by both SeatPlan and Headout. Because there is no balcony above, front-mezz rows have zero overhang.

SeatPlan calls Center Mezzanine rows C-F the value pick - 'enough rake to see over the top of heads' at sub-premium pricing - and because Broadhurst has no balcony above, the rear mezzanine is not overhung itself. The back four rows are slightly shorter with a decent rake, and a Tripadvisor reviewer (Apr 2024) reported a 'crystal clear view' from the last row of the mezzanine.
